html:
Emperor Wu, born Liu Che, ruled China's Han dynasty from 141 to 87 BCE. His reign of 54 years, one of the longest in Chinese history, was the Han at its most warlike and ambitious.

  • War: he ended the old policy of buying peace from the Xiongnu with brides and gifts. From 133 BCE he sent huge cavalry armies onto the steppe and pushed them back north of the Gobi.
  • Conquest: his armies took Nanyue in the south in 111 BCE, Minyue in 110 BCE and Gojoseon in Korea in 108 BCE, and set up commanderies along the Gansu corridor.
  • The west: he sent Zhang Qian to Central Asia, and later fought the War of the Heavenly Horses against Ferghana for its horses. This opened the routes later called the Silk Road.
  • Ideas: he made Confucian learning the state's official teaching and founded an imperial academy to train officials in the classics.
  • Money: to pay for the wars he made salt and iron state monopolies, a policy argued over in the Discourses on Salt and Iron after his death.

His last years were dark. In 91 BCE a witchcraft scare at court ended in the death of his crown prince. The historian Sima Qian wrote his great history under Wu, after the emperor had him castrated for defending a defeated general.
sum: Emperor Wu, born Liu Che, ruled China's Han dynasty from 141 to 87 BCE. His reign of 54 years, one of the longest in Chinese history, was the Han at its most warlike and ambitious.
